paragraphs.text: V. [A THANKSGIVING CONCERNING HIS OWN LIFE.] IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER AND OF THE SON AND OF THE HOLY SPIRIT.

It is the pronouncement of the most learned teacher of the Gentiles that our weakness gives birth to power, and that the soul grows strong when the earthly is crushed. For then the strength that has flowed from the substance of the flesh runs to the spirit, and our very weakening fashions the heavenly man, who is to be set in the divine citadel, and brings him to the fruit of the spirit. So, when bodies are left without cultivation or harvest, it is sweet, and when they are diminished for the sake of increase, we arrive at the rich grace of God through a fasting and barren poverty of the limbs. Therefore it is to you, our weakness, that we owe it, after God, that we have risen up to a love of sublime things. The welcome compulsion of my fever, and the burning of my marrow, which I must embrace, taught me both to fear God when my health departed and to rejoice in him when it returned. Now the health of mind won through sickness rejoices in our Maker. Where is that pride in long-lasting health, which earned only mockery? Where is the haughtiness that made you believe God's gift was your own possession? Suddenly the firmness of your strength deserted you, and, bowed beneath the weight of sickness, you lay there with your neck broken. Now that your prosperity has fled, you ponder a late repentance and recognize that your strength belonged to our God. Thanks be to you, Ruler and Creator of heaven, who by a subtle dispensation and by hidden paths of mercy order our ways even through affliction, and by a loving laceration restore us to perfect virtue. We cannot come to your healing except with the help of a wound, for when you strike us we learn to soften the hardness of our hearts, and to crush the promptings of earthly baseness by the noble and most sweet suffering of our troubles.

Behold, I am the man who used to applaud himself for a vigour that had lasted him so long. While I enjoyed it without a break, as though no interruption would ever end it, I used to wonder how death, the wages of sin, could ever come. For, puffed up by mad successes, I had enrolled myself in the flock of poets, ignorant of the venerable profession I had taken up. I took delight in poems built of squared parts and made solid by an ordered variety of feet. A flowing or tender poem set me among the choirs of angels, and if I happened to have composed brilliant verses while keeping the rules, I saw whatever lies beneath the vault of heaven set under my feet. Mortal life long tossed me about in my folly, and a certain blindness to my miseries carried me away [?] on a false felicity of speech. How often did my head, shaven for religion's sake, swell with the breath of those who acclaimed me, and believe, through the lying enticements of playful lips, that it ruled over the hearts of those who loved it? But you, who dwell in the heavens, laughed at me: you, who are won over not by words but by purity; you, before whom we often speak when silent and are silent when we shout. So, while the charm of superfluous elegance drove me through the fields of rhetoric and poetry, I had followed a lying wisdom and departed from the true, desiring nothing but to rise on the breezes of empty praise. I had a distaste for prayer, while I was held fast by the desire to make speeches and to trade [?]. Wretched man that I am! Who would restore me from the body of this death? The grace of God, granted through the ministry of a curable disease. For behold, pain suddenly entered the seat of my terrified soul and fed on the secret places of my heart with a hostile fire. Then all that makes a man wasted away in a constant burning, and the heat within broke out through the natural passages. While arrogance was being driven out of its hiding places, though I still kept something of the vain man, I had nothing left of the living man. Of a living man's awareness only this remained: the confidence that I could be healed by you, my God, whom I had provoked to anger by my error. Nor did that ravaging plague, my teacher, lie hidden once it had been sent into the chambers of my innards; not content to stay concealed, it had clothed me wholly in a cloud of sallow colour, so that what in other illnesses is sought out by the fingers of physicians, the common people could see displayed for their own correction. My long calamity burned those who loved me, and it burned my enemies; some were tormented by despair at my death, others by its nearness. The city was of one verdict, though divided in its sympathies.

Meanwhile a devouring fire was ravaging me in its work within, and it was fed by the constant efforts of those who tended me. For whatever was provided against the disease only increased it, as though it were nourishing it. Then that philosophy of worldly pomp, worn down by the remedies of Hippocrates and Galen, turned to faithful help, perceiving at last that the world's blandishments vanish and that a man is not helped by human defences. By now the pressure of this disaster had held me in subjection for the course of nearly two months. By now I was awaiting death in place of a cure, and, finding nothing sweet as I looked back on the use of this light, I longed to cut short the delay, even though I would go laden with the burden of sin. Weigh, you who read, what scourges, what torments awaited me here, that fear of present punishments made me seek out the pains of hell, and hasten to the expiations of that undying furnace that breathes out such dread. But the Lord did not fail me in his majesty, he who kills and makes alive, who brings down to the underworld and brings back again, he whose promise it is: "While the words are still in your mouth, behold, I am here, says the Lord." For one of those who sat by me, and who day by day lavished my fortune on my sickness, declared that he was exhausted and that nothing remained to be done; and at once the physician's despair brought me hope of life. For the blessings of heavenly help are readiest when the ill-starred services of men have been withdrawn from the sick. Straightaway I had myself carried to the protection of the blessed martyr Victor, which I had often experienced, and having prayed for the help of that bravest of men, I entrusted to him with tears what he was to plead before God for me: that it was enough to win God's mercy if he always kept before his eyes the stuff from which he had taken us, and remembered that the lowest matter cannot easily pass with speed to the loftiness of his commandments. Although through the second, loving birth of baptism all the filth we contracted from our parent clay has been washed away, yet the enemy of our salvation paints over the ruin he hides within his blandishments and has seasoned vices with a sweet taste; and while we are led on by the itching of the ears [?] and the pleasure of tasting, death comes in through the windows. Where, then, are we to flee from God's wrath, if not to the mercy of him who called back the returning son, the prodigal of his granted portion? Though unclean fellowship had bound that son to the swine and to the foul food of husks, the father recalled him to the white robe, to the precious ring, to the riches of his father's estate, as though he had always kept his commands. Through God's chosen one I prayed that he would forgive me my many debts, so that, once absolved, I might show him greater love. And appealing to the bond of his promise with a chaste pledge, I asked also that he would grant me to run through his precepts with loving devotion. For although it is his doing that we are called, and his doing that, once called, we consent, he rewards these things as though they had sprung from us; he himself prompts us both to will what is right and to accomplish it, and yet he gives the prize as though he were indebted to our devotion. I promised too that, if by his grace he endowed me with a love of nobler study, this confession would proceed from the hand of my tongue; that I would offer to him the fat of my poor talent, which is itself his gift, so that the care of my pen would never again weary itself with the windy treatment of worldly things; and that I would also renounce the other foul things by which I was disfigured, provided that he himself, who inspired me to say this, would make me will it. I begged him to stand by me with his benefits and not to turn away from one whom he had mercifully cherished when he was left without the protection of his own kin, and whom he had preferred to those who rejoiced in the defence of their parents. And in granting these things he did not repay my innocence, but showed how much a fortunate and well-taught sinner owes to his grace. For if, in following mercy, he did not set aside the strict guarding of justice, and if he terrified us as a judge instead of cherishing us as a father, no way of salvation, no path of escape would lie open anywhere.

My God, my redemption, what things come to my mind of all that you have done for me, and what of all that I have done against myself? If they were compared, no moment would be found empty either of your help or of my sin. From your countless gifts to me I would like to take one sample and, passing over the multitudes of your bounties, touch lightly on a single one. At the time when the longed-for arrival of King Theoderic revived Italy, when everything was being laid waste by his enemies with indescribable slaughter, and famine killed whatever the sword had spared, when want broke through the lofty strongholds of mountains and fortresses, and need, crueller than arms, besieged those who had settled on the heights, I, at about sixteen years of age, was in that storm deprived of the comfort of my aunt, who had raised me. I was left alone, without means and without counsel, a youth to whom only adversity could offer a remedy. So that I should not, though free, have to beg the means of living among my kinsfolk, which is more bitter than the lot of captivity, nor, though known to all, endure the hardships of strangers, at once you stretched out your accustomed right hand, my defender, and moved a house rich in wealth and in religion not to spurn me in my need. I asked for the little daughter of a certain most noble lady, well known to you, in marriage, and was at once accepted, for you arranged that it should be granted before I asked, as though it were what I ought to have been hoping for. The fellowship of those who please you brought me both an abundance of sustenance and a way of passing to your worship, fleeing the darkness of unbelief. Almost before I recognized my desolation, gifts began to be supplied to me in plenty. Then, changed for the first time from beggar into king, I began to mock the miseries of the afflicted, and, as though prosperity had been my due, to disregard the author of those blessings. Yet you did not at once crush the rebel spirit and the swelling of my stiff neck. You put off the time of vengeance, to see whether perhaps I might be stung to remorse and, being healed, might at least perceive who the giver was. But because a man is not reformed from injustice, nor easily brought back to whiteness after being stained, I held to that resolve of mine by which I was to fall, and I outlasted your patience by persisting in sin. And because, most merciful as you are, you do not always set justice aside, I was stripped of your protection and heard that voice which was directed to the ears of our first parent: "Adam, where are you?" In my confusion I counted up how many treasures of your mercy I had lost and of what dowry I had been stripped. I was granted a true estimate of the things you had bestowed only when they were perishing for me. I came back to myself and to my troubles, and I wept for the joys I had squandered. At once you came to my aid by another road, but no lesser one. You ordained that I should be healed by being compelled into the office of the Levites, and that the burden of the honour thrust upon me should remove the weight that pressed me down. But after the weight of that venerable dignity had set me free, I took pride in the title, but had no conscience formed by the brightness of my conduct. O mind, drunk with a poisonous hardness, taught neither by examples nor by warnings! If you lack the teaching of venerable books, be shaped for progress by punishments; and unless you plunge yourself into the mire of perdition, you can draw instruction from your penalty. But may he who commands these things work them in us, and, that we may prove equal to his commands, may he himself work with us what he enjoins.

These things and many more, as I said before, I submitted to be made known through that most approved witness, the blessed Victor; and neither rest nor delay slackened what was to be obtained. He took up my petition, presented it, and won it. My advocate even obtained more than I had asked: that she who had been joined to me in the equal yoke of marriage should share with me the honours of the religious state, and that a woman should lead the way to a glorious title. But would that I followed her, frail in sex as she is, in strength of mind, and that in noble action she did not surpass me in merit as far as, by reason of womanly weakness, she seems to come after me! By the vigour of a precious constancy she utterly subdued the well-known evils of the flesh, and kept a chastity that was loving, not forced. By loving the observance of what is right so steadfastly, she compelled it to become her nature. Would that she may not be set against me in the hour of strict judgment, and that, while she has shown herself strong in her weakness, I may not be found frail in my natural strength! Behold, Lord, I have recounted the very things you already knew, and I have been faithful only in this respect, that I have not seized what was yours. Be with me, King of glory, be with one who prays to you, and according to the custom of your kindness, order what is to follow.
GLORY BE TO THE FATHER AND TO THE SON AND TO THE HOLY SPIRIT.
